chunks: "Sure. For two inputs there are four rows, so I list A and B as 00, 01, 10, 11, and then fill in each gate. NOT has one input: 0 gives 1, 1 gives 0.
AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, so the column is 0, 0, 0, 1. OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1: 0, 1, 1, 1.
NAND is just AND inverted, so 1, 1, 1, 0, and NOR is OR inverted: 1, 0, 0, 0.
XOR is 1 when the inputs differ: 0, 1, 1, 0, and XNOR is the opposite, 1 when they're equal: 1, 0, 0, 1. I don't memorize the columns.
I remember one sentence per gate: AND needs all ones, OR needs at least one one, XOR needs an odd number of ones, and the N versions are the complement.
For more inputs the table grows to 2 to the n rows and the same sentences still work.
For example 3-input AND has only the 111 row high, and 3-input XOR is high on 001, 010, 100, and 111, so it's parity, not 'exactly one'.
One useful way to think about it: for AND the controlling value is 0, for OR it's 1, and XOR has none, it just acts like a conditional inverter."
